Art Theft

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South africa is a mecca for art thieves, Carte Blanche delves into the art theft world - how they do it, where they sell it, and ask why art is one of the best illicit currency's in the world.

Unique Selling Point:
we have the footage of an art heist at Davielle Ballie gallery when it was still in Norwood. It has since moved to Jeppe and is in an up-and-coming artistic area – we will be filming the interviews there in a beautiful backdrop of artwork and creativity. We can interview Darren (owner)/Matthew (curator) from the gallery about the theft that will be shown on the TV. They are happy to accommodate all our interviews there, as we can film links there as well. They are seeing if we can speak to the artist whose works were specifically targeted – the footage shows men entering the premises pretending to be security guards, once inside, they take out guns and go for the art work they specifically wanted.
John Pearson (art investigator) will break down the theft and speak about what happened after – he says they then went to a nearby house, and couldn’t find a buyer. They then contacted a local artist who sells his art at Killarney Mall, he took the paintings, not knowing they were stolen, and was sitting with them to sell. He recognized that one of them had a number of the back, and it was the gallery – they then sent Pearson to go and see – all 5 paintings worth R500,000 were recovered.
There are lots of other cases in South Africa regarding art theft – one of the most perplexing was the one where Ace Magashule gave a Pierneef work R2.5 million to a bodyguard when he was moving office. The bodyguard gave it to an auction house, that recognized it and returned the painting.


Summary:
Art theft is not a common crime, but when the thieves hit, they hit big – often amounting to millions of irreplaceable stolen art or artifacts.
According to Robert Pearson, of Pearson and associates, the expert investigators of art thefts (specific) there are various kinds of thieves – 1. opportunists who see it as an easy buck, but are often caught because they don’t know where to sell it, and often end up getting caught by auction houses or pawn shops, these paintings are sometimes destroyed/abandoned to void being caught with the artwork and sometimes end up in private homes for display purposes And 2. Selective targeting of specific pieces, artists, museums and collectors. This can take place at museums, galleries, and private residences.
All thefts are limited due to security, often theft by a trust employee who forms a close relationship with the target is a common trend. Pearson has a good network of contacts to circulate the details of a piece with reward money often, often resulting in recoveries.
There are some preventative measures: security, good CCTV camera surveillance, motion detected surveillance. Exhibitions, auctions and private viewings that are advertised tend to lure in the criminal element – we need to be careful without program.
International criminals are known to frequent SA, and through local crime syndicates, identify and target arts and private collections – either well-known or up and coming artists, as well as specific collections.



Further information:
Enter our police force Dr. Bernadine Benson is a professor at UNISA, but has been at the forefront of art crime since the late 1990’s. She is very energetic when she speaks about art – she will explain the history of art theft in our country, and she had several funny examples – wife selling priceless painting. She has written several articles and is often the person the police go to to understand the criminal who may have been behind the theft. She added that art is often used to launder or clean dirty money.
Enter Interpol agent Estie von Hagen who will talk about art theft internationally and how art is used to smuggle money and facilitate illicit activities. That another level and element to art crime.
Dr. Bernice Hagen will speak about how South Africa has no asset register, and we can bring that admission up from our last story – and she will talk about how museums do not have security and therefore many do not show you any art work – you have to ask to see the collection and make an appointment, and even then you are guaranteed to see it.
She will also talk a little bit about forgeries and how that impacts the industry.
Lastly another layer is that we will speak to Gordon Massie – the head of Art Insure – they are the only insurance company that insure artwork. They have a list of artworks stolen, and it is the only list in the country – together with Pearson they have the most amount of knowledge of current art works and value in the country. He will tell us about private collections and other case studies.
I met with Flo Bird who just reaffirmed my position on government museums – we don’t need to interview her, but a lot of museums are uninsured (as Pearson will tell us) and because there is no security or asset register this three tiered combo makes south Africa the mecca for art thieves.
Museums as case studies:
Stolen Picasso at JAG – which Dr. Hagen will speak about – never recovered
Stolen Kentridge which Pearson will speak about it – recovered at auction house
SA artist who stole 17.5 million (3 paintings) from a Pretoria museum – caught and prosecuted, very high profile case
I have gone to William Kentridge’s gallery on Main to see if I can find him, trying to get him on board to be interviewed, the gallery we are working with are also speaking to the artist whose paintings were stolen in our story – but he has an identity that he has hidden from the public eye and would likely want to be hidden – which might just add to his mystique.

Press Release:


Art Theft
Art theft is not a common crime, but when the thieves hit, they hit big – taking expensive paintings and drawings and selling them on the black market. Carte Blanche delves into the criminal underbelly of art theft and reveals why this is one of the most favoured illicit currencies in the world.
Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein
Presenter: Derek Watts
Research: Sinethemba Nogude
Watch the trailer



Script:


When you think of great works of art many think of London, Paris, New York and Italy. But South Africa is fast becoming a Mecca for art collectors looking for master pieces to add to their private houses or galleries. And where this is great art, the art thieves follow.
ART HEISTS ARE BECOMING MORE COMMON AROUND SOUTH AFRICA...WE MAY NOT HAVE THE MONA LISAS OF THE WORLD BUT OUR OWN ARTISTS ARE FETCHING GOOD PRICES AND THE CRIMINAL ELEMENTS HAVE SEEN THE GAP.
[Video of break-in…]
This CCTV footage shows an art theft in progress at the Daville Baillie
(DA ville Bailey) Gallery in Johannesburg.
Darren: “Some guys came into gallery walked around - easier to sell - higher in value. At 4pm that afternoon, gallery robbed at gunpoint.”
Gallery owner Darren Neofytou (neo – fe-toe) says the criminals were disguised as security guards and chose carefully ……
- watch as they even pick up and put back down art they don’t want.
THESE WERE SOPHISTICATED CRIMINALS WHO KNEW WHAT THEY WANTED... PIECES SIMILAR TO THE PAINTINGS ON DISPLAY HERE AT THE GALLERY'S NEW VENUE IN THE SOUTH OF JOHANNESBURG
Darren: “They walked in, one guy held the two people at gunpoint, and the other two were pointed in direction of art works.
John: “The art world is obviously a finer area, and it’s more selective, the criminals know what they want, and they normally steal to order.”
Loss adjuster John Pearson the Managing Director of Pearson and Associates made his name investigating violent crimes like cash & transit heists. He knows art thieves operate differently.
Pearson: “We’ve had quite a substantial loss from a private dwelling house - where they went in posing as contractors, they selected a valuable painting - and some months later we received information that it was at a well fortified house in Soweto, and we recovered the painting.”
The Daville Baillie heist resulted in half a million rand’s worth of art stolen. Pearson investigated.
John: “They knew were cameras were, they had a vehicles waiting outside.”
But then 6 months later the paintings resurfaced.
John: “Information came into the gallery owner, a sketch artist had come across a painting that they believed had originated from that gallery. It took me to a shopping centre, I did surveillance on the sketch artist, I noticed, next to his desk that there were paintings lined-up. and we recovered all 5 paintings that were stolen in good condition.”
ITOO Artinsure is South Africa’s only specialist provider of insurance for art and collectables, underwritten by the Hollard Insurance Company. Managing director Gordon Massie explains how insurance of art works.
Derek: “What happens when stolen pieces and the person is paid out, and then the painting reappears?”
Gordon: “Once we’ve paid out indemnity for a client, it belongs to the insurers, so we give them the opportunity to buy back from us. I would say, 90% of private collectors want to buy the item from us on recovery.”
Derek: “Are most private collections fully insured?”
Gordon: “No, I would estimate that 40% are insurance adequately.”
Darren: “Art up until now, it seems to have flown under the radar, people are not really aware of the value, and I believe in the past few years targeted.”
Darren says thieves often target up-and-coming artists: two of the paintings stolen belonged to a pop artist named “Fringe.”
Darren: “He’s an anonymous artist and because of his anonymity, the team that is involved selects a different celebrity each year, to play the role of fringe in the public persona, so in 2018, Fringe has been played by Danny k.”
After speaking to “Fringe” at the gallery, Musician Danny K - in his role as fringe - relayed how the theft made the artist feel.
Danny k: “Every work, is unique, every work really is a piece of me and once it’s gone, it’s gone forever…”
IT’S NOT ONLY THE PRIVATE GALLERIES BUT PUBLIC MUSEUMS AND SPACES WHICH HOUSE SOME OF THE COUNTRY'S MOST VALUED AND PRICELESS PIECES. WITHOUT A LOT OF ATTENTION TO PRESERVING THEM.
Public museums and galleries are often underfunded, and therefore understaffed, leading to a lack of security measures. But adding to that, is the fact that it was only last year that government began the tremendous task of compiling a national asset register, so, before, when art went missing, sometimes it went unnoticed.
While that process will take time, to aid in recoveries, the insurers came up with a solution - an art theft register.
Gordon: “It was in response to there being no meaningful centralized data in South Africa so nowhere where somebody could go to check if the work was stolen art work, before they try and sell it.”
Dr. Bernadine Benson studied the criminals behind these thefts while she served as a police officer for 19 years.
Bernadine: “One art theft is one too many, because there is only one of a kind.”
Derek: “When we look at art theft, is it opportunistic or experts?”
Bernadine: “They say that a theft would happen is there’s a perpetrator, motivated person, an item that can be stolen and an incapable guardian and the majority of incidents’ is usually from opportunistic thefts.”
But there have been targeted thefts - like these Asian ceramics at a Pretoria museum.
Bernadine: “The thieves came in they took a lot of things, 2 months later, they went back and stole the rest of the things.”
Derek: “How does a thief get rid of at a good price, a work of art, especially if it’s by a well-known artist?”
Beradine: “He’s not. He’s going to get rid of it, it’s too hot.”
As was the case in 2006 where a Pierneef was stolen by a man out of government building.
Bernadine: “He had the painting he tried to cut it up to sell it as pierneefs, and immediately the dealer saw there was something, and this frightened the guy and he burnt it, and then we lost it, it’s gone.”
ACCORDING TO INTERPOL, INTERNATIONAL CRIMINALS ARE KNOWN TO TARGET VALUABLE COLLECTIONS... AND ART CAN BE USED AS AN IDEAL WAY TO LAUNDER DIRTY MONEY.
As hard to prove as this is, research shows that stolen South African art is sold more successfully overseas.
Bernadine: “If it’s too famous, it will probably disappear, if it’s not famous enough, then it can go abroad and sell unfortunately relatively easy in European and British Markets.”
In some cases the perpetrator is caught out by the auctioneers - as was the case when a client’s wife approached an auction house during her divorce.
Bernadine: “What happened was the wife had the painting sold, or offered on auction, because she was angry with her husband. So she had a fake made, which hung in the house and he didn’t know...”
Derek: “Fraud is another aspect that must come into your universe?
Gordon: “I’m afraid that the number of forgers, and the number of entrance of works, into the secondary market, is increasing.”
You might be mistaken for thinking this is a real.
Gordon: “It was sold at auction, the buyer thought it was a Stanley Pinker when the conservator went to clean it, we found out it was a Stanley Plonker and valueless.”
Auctioneers Stephan Welz & Co held an art auction this week.
Upsound Auction: points and says - “R80,000.”
Anton Welz who heads the auction house, says forgeries and fakes are costing millions.
Anton: “We’ve had van Wouw, Kentridge, Boshof, pinker - and that's just that's just what we've seen coming through our doors. So there on it’s own is probably two million rands worth of work that we've seen as fake or forgery.”
Last year, several fakes were uncovered like this one which had been painted over a print and where the pixels are visible under a blue light.
Dr Benson: “You can test it at home, if you do your nail polish, if you run the bluelight over it, you can see where the changes have been affected.”
Anton: “What's happening more and more is that you're seeing works turning up on auctions in England in America. All of a sudden it's got a little bit of a provenance it's got a little bit of a history and now it's almost legit.”
Another fake was this Anton van Wouw which is a cast of a cast …astonishingly these are all fakes nearly sold on auction.
Danny K as “Fringe” says the artist felt robbed of his creation.
Danny K: “I think any creative person will agree that you create to give, and when it’s taken its not really in the spirit of which art is ever created.”
Art is priceless… but art theft shows that value isn’t only in the price tag.

But adding to that, is the fact that it was only last year that government began the tremendous task of compiling a national asset register, so, before, when art went missing, sometimes it went unnoticed. While that process will take time, to aid in recoveries, the insurers came up with a solution - an art theft register. Gordon: “It was in response to there being no meaningful centralized data in South Africa so nowhere where somebody could go to check if the work was stolen art work, before they try and sell it.” Dr. Bernadine Benson studied the criminals behind these thefts while she served as a police officer for 19 years. Bernadine: “One art theft is one too many, because there is only one of a kind.” Derek: “When we look at art theft, is it opportunistic or experts?” Bernadine: “They say that a theft would happen is there’s a perpetrator, motivated person, an item that can be stolen and an incapable guardian and the majority of incidents’ is usually from opportunistic thefts.” But there have been targeted thefts - like these Asian ceramics at a Pretoria museum. Bernadine: “The thieves came in they took a lot of things, 2 months later, they went back and stole the rest of the things.” Derek: “How does a thief get rid of at a good price, a work of art, especially if it’s by a well-known artist?” Beradine: “He’s not. He’s going to get rid of it, it’s too hot.” As was the case in 2006 where a Pierneef was stolen by a man out of government building. Bernadine: “He had the painting he tried to cut it up to sell it as pierneefs, and immediately the dealer saw there was something, and this frightened the guy and he burnt it, and then we lost it, it’s gone.” ACCORDING TO INTERPOL, INTERNATIONAL CRIMINALS ARE KNOWN TO TARGET VALUABLE COLLECTIONS... AND ART CAN BE USED AS AN IDEAL WAY TO LAUNDER DIRTY MONEY. As hard to prove as this is, research shows that stolen South African art is sold more successfully overseas. Bernadine: “If it’s too famous, it will probably disappear, if it’s not famous enough, then it can go abroad and sell unfortunately relatively easy in European and British Markets.” In some cases the perpetrator is caught out by the auctioneers - as was the case when a client’s wife approached an auction house during her divorce. Bernadine: “What happened was the wife had the painting sold, or offered on auction, because she was angry with her husband. So she had a fake made, which hung in the house and he didn’t know...” Derek: “Fraud is another aspect that must come into your universe? Gordon: “I’m afraid that the number of forgers, and the number of entrance of works, into the secondary market, is increasing.” You might be mistaken for thinking this is a real. Gordon: “It was sold at auction, the buyer thought it was a Stanley Pinker when the conservator went to clean it, we found out it was a Stanley Plonker and valueless.” Auctioneers Stephan Welz & Co held an art auction this week. Upsound Auction: points and says - “R80,000.” Anton Welz who heads the auction house, says forgeries and fakes are costing millions. Anton: “We’ve had van Wouw, Kentridge, Boshof, pinker - and that's just that's just what we've seen coming through our doors. So there on it’s own is probably two million rands worth of work that we've seen as fake or forgery.” Last year, several fakes were uncovered like this one which had been painted over a print and where the pixels are visible under a blue light. Dr Benson: “You can test it at home, if you do your nail polish, if you run the bluelight over it, you can see where the changes have been affected.” Anton: “What's happening more and more is that you're seeing works turning up on auctions in England in America. All of a sudden it's got a little bit of a provenance it's got a little bit of a history and now it's almost legit.” Another fake was this Anton van Wouw which is a cast of a cast …astonishingly these are all fakes nearly sold on auction. Danny K as “Fringe” says the artist felt robbed of his creation. Danny K: “I think any creative person will agree that you create to give, and when it’s taken its not really in the spirit of which art is ever created.” Art is priceless… but art theft shows that value isn’t only in the price tag.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): South africa is a mecca for art thieves, Carte Blanche delves into the art theft world - how they do it, where they sell it, and ask why art is one of the best illicit currency's in the world.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: we have the footage of an art heist at Davielle Ballie gallery when it was still in Norwood. It has since moved to Jeppe and is in an up-and-coming artistic area – we will be filming the interviews there in a beautiful backdrop of artwork and creativity. We can interview Darren (owner)/Matthew (curator) from the gallery about the theft that will be shown on the TV. They are happy to accommodate all our interviews there, as we can film links there as well. They are seeing if we can speak to the artist whose works were specifically targeted – the footage shows men entering the premises pretending to be security guards, once inside, they take out guns and go for the art work they specifically wanted. John Pearson (art investigator) will break down the theft and speak about what happened after – he says they then went to a nearby house, and couldn’t find a buyer. They then contacted a local artist who sells his art at Killarney Mall, he took the paintings, not knowing they were stolen, and was sitting with them to sell. He recognized that one of them had a number of the back, and it was the gallery – they then sent Pearson to go and see – all 5 paintings worth R500,000 were recovered. There are lots of other cases in South Africa regarding art theft – one of the most perplexing was the one where Ace Magashule gave a Pierneef work R2.5 million to a bodyguard when he was moving office. The bodyguard gave it to an auction house, that recognized it and returned the painting.
metadata.Summary: Art theft is not a common crime, but when the thieves hit, they hit big – often amounting to millions of irreplaceable stolen art or artifacts. According to Robert Pearson, of Pearson and associates, the expert investigators of art thefts (specific) there are various kinds of thieves – 1. opportunists who see it as an easy buck, but are often caught because they don’t know where to sell it, and often end up getting caught by auction houses or pawn shops, these paintings are sometimes destroyed/abandoned to void being caught with the artwork and sometimes end up in private homes for display purposes And 2. Selective targeting of specific pieces, artists, museums and collectors. This can take place at museums, galleries, and private residences. All thefts are limited due to security, often theft by a trust employee who forms a close relationship with the target is a common trend. Pearson has a good network of contacts to circulate the details of a piece with reward money often, often resulting in recoveries. There are some preventative measures: security, good CCTV camera surveillance, motion detected surveillance. Exhibitions, auctions and private viewings that are advertised tend to lure in the criminal element – we need to be careful without program. International criminals are known to frequent SA, and through local crime syndicates, identify and target arts and private collections – either well-known or up and coming artists, as well as specific collections.
metadata.Further information: Enter our police force Dr. Bernadine Benson is a professor at UNISA, but has been at the forefront of art crime since the late 1990’s. She is very energetic when she speaks about art – she will explain the history of art theft in our country, and she had several funny examples – wife selling priceless painting. She has written several articles and is often the person the police go to to understand the criminal who may have been behind the theft. She added that art is often used to launder or clean dirty money. Enter Interpol agent Estie von Hagen who will talk about art theft internationally and how art is used to smuggle money and facilitate illicit activities. That another level and element to art crime. Dr. Bernice Hagen will speak about how South Africa has no asset register, and we can bring that admission up from our last story – and she will talk about how museums do not have security and therefore many do not show you any art work – you have to ask to see the collection and make an appointment, and even then you are guaranteed to see it. She will also talk a little bit about forgeries and how that impacts the industry. Lastly another layer is that we will speak to Gordon Massie – the head of Art Insure – they are the only insurance company that insure artwork. They have a list of artworks stolen, and it is the only list in the country – together with Pearson they have the most amount of knowledge of current art works and value in the country. He will tell us about private collections and other case studies. I met with Flo Bird who just reaffirmed my position on government museums – we don’t need to interview her, but a lot of museums are uninsured (as Pearson will tell us) and because there is no security or asset register this three tiered combo makes south Africa the mecca for art thieves. Museums as case studies: Stolen Picasso at JAG – which Dr. Hagen will speak about – never recovered Stolen Kentridge which Pearson will speak about it – recovered at auction house SA artist who stole 17.5 million (3 paintings) from a Pretoria museum – caught and prosecuted, very high profile case I have gone to William Kentridge’s gallery on Main to see if I can find him, trying to get him on board to be interviewed, the gallery we are working with are also speaking to the artist whose paintings were stolen in our story – but he has an identity that he has hidden from the public eye and would likely want to be hidden – which might just add to his mystique.
